utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Registrar would you now please have the accused brought in? (The accused was brought in).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody hear? Is everybody ready? Mr. Kehoe, are you expecting your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President and your Honours. The usher went to get Mr. Djidic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a point of order, the Trial Chamber is -- it is important that the organisation of the proceedings be correct, about how long do you plan to question your witness, all morning long? We have some delay here, which has nothing to do with our own will. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Djidic will probably testify until some time mid to late afternoon, possibly until the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Tomorrow morning, we do not meet. Therefore, we will resume in the afternoon, and all day on Thursday. Right. I think that you can go ahead now 23 MR. SEFJIKA DJIDIC cont'd Examined-in-chief by MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, do you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. I hear very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. Looking to your left Mr. Djidic you mentioned yesterday there was a conflict in Novi Travnik. Could you point that city out on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very good. Everybody can see. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to clarify Mr. Djidic on that particular map, the name of Novi Travnik is Pucarevo, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when the judges look at the map and see Pucarevo that is the same as Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, yesterday we ended off and you were talking about a checkpoint in mid to late October 1992, where HVO troops attempted to get through the checkpoint on the way to Novi Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where was that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That checkpoint was near the village of Ahmici at the threshold of Vitez. At the other end of Vitez there was a standing checkpoint held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina inside Vitez, more precisely at the railway station there was an HVO checkpoint, and there were many other local checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this checkpoint in Ahmici, tell us what happened when the HVO tried to get through that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The checkpoint operated for a brief period of time, HVO chased out members of the Territorial Defence, and HVO passed through. After that the locals from the village of Ahmici received an ultimatum to give up their weapons, and they did so, meaning that the village of Ahmici was disbanded. On the same day the villagers of Donja Veceriska also received an ultimatum to give up their weapons. One soldier of the HVO named Petar Mecava who was commander of HVO units in Donja Veceriska told members of the Territorial Defence that a decision had been taken by the HVO that all Muslims had to give up their arms. However, the villagers of Donja Veceriska refused to do so. The situation was similar in all of Vitez, all members of the Territorial Defence were required, by the HVO, to give up their weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately when did this event take place, this disarming, of the residents of Ahmici and the confrontation at the checkpoint in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened on the 18th, 19th and 20th October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After the conflict in Novi Travnik did there begin to be conflict in the City, in the town of Vitez, and especially involving the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. International factors such as the UNPROFOR and members of the International Monitoring Mission set up meetings with HVO and the Territorial Defence, which in those two or three days that the -- of crisis, were held at one meeting when we were there with the HVO in the afternoon. I think it was on the 20th October. Suddenly we heard loud shooting, and when we went outside we were in front of the building of the post office where the meeting was held. I saw that my logistics department had been attacked. Mr. Ivica Santic told members of the UNPROFOR: "Look, we are being attacked by the Muslims". And that was not correct, because an hour later we found out that the logistics of the Territorial Defence was attacked, and members of the Territorial Defence were arrested and taken to the Vitez hotel. There were seven men imprisoned and the house holding the logistics department was demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where did Blaskic have his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, the headquarters was situated at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Hotel Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the usher's permission if we could take down the map which is Exhibit 29, and there is a photograph that has been previously received in evidence as Prosecutor's Exhibit 56, that is clipped to the board. That is the next exhibit that we will be moving to. Actually, Mr. Dubuisson, if we could use Exhibit 45 first. Could we use Exhibit 45 first? Could we put that up, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, using Exhibit 45, could you use the pointer once again and step up to the map, and with the -- point to the area, first, of the Hotel Vitez and then where your logistics centre was that was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Hotel Vitez (Indicates). As I said, this is Hotel Vitez (Indicates). And this was where my logistics centre was (Indicates), used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, can you hear me okay with that new set of headphones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was attacked after your logistics centre was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the attack on the logistics centre, next came my headquarters, which was situated here (Indicates). It was shot at from infantry weapons. Then there was a cease-fire, when we agreed, at the same meeting, to go out into the field. We agreed for a joint commission to go out into the field, to have an exchange of prisoners, and to remove all checkpoints in Vitez; and that is what we did. The commission consisted of, on the part of the HVO, Mario Cerkez and the local priest. On the part of the Territorial Defence, there was myself and the local Hodza, Muslim priest. We tried to convince people to remove all checkpoints, because there was a checkpoint in every village, both Croatian and Muslim; and we managed to persuade them; and in the meantime the exchange of prisoners took place. Seven prisoners, seven members of the Territorial Defence, and one member of the HVO were released. All members of the Territorial Defence had visible traces of mistreatment on their bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where had those seven prisoners been taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven prisoners were released to go home from the Territorial Defence, and one prisoner who was a member of the HVO was brought from Krusica and brought to the Vitez hotel without any visible trace of abuse on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, you said that the members of the Territorial Defence that had been abused had been -- had been taken to a particular location after they had been arrested, where were they taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had been taken to the Vitez hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You can sit down, sir. After this series of events, did you have -- continue to have meetings with members of the HVO concerning ways to settle the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The meetings continued. On the same night, after having done our business, we went to the hotel bar. I was there representing the Territorial Defence. There were also members of the UNPROFOR, the International Monitoring Mission, and of the HVO. I remained there for about an hour or two, and when I meant to leave the HVO suggested that I take an escort with me, an HVO soldier, who very politely escorted me to the cross-roads, where from the road led to the logistics centre. I walked alone to the logistics centre, made sure that there was -- found out there was nobody there from the Territorial Defence. Then I came back to my own headquarters, which was also empty at the time. I noted that the headquarters were evicted from the school. Members of the Territorial Defence left in the direction of Stari Vitez, while we were removing checkpoints. On the following day, and for several days to follow, negotiations continued at which the HVO demanded that all Muslim members of the Territorial Defence of Vitez give up their arms and place themselves under the command of the HVO. We were given an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who gave you that ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ultimatum was communicated to me by Mario Cerkez. He told me that the government of the HVO had a session, and decided that Muslims had to give up their arms before the 24th at noon. I think it was the 24th, or maybe the 25th, I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have any questions with the individual that you talked about yesterday, Pero Skopljak? Did he discuss this matter with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. At the time when the negotiations were held, Pero Skopljak played a prominent part, and at one point he said that if the army, that is the Territorial Defence, refused to place themselves under the command of the HVO, we would have a fight, and he also said that Muslims did not stand a chance, that HVO was much stronger and that we had to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was the HVO much stronger, at that time, in Vitez? And if they were, why were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, they were not significantly stronger, they were stronger, because they had no soldiers on the front line against the Chetniks, whereas members of the Territorial Defence, who had the best weapons, the best arms, and the best fighters, were, at that time, engaged in Visoko and in Vlasic on the front lines. A small group of the HVO was deployed in positions against the Chetniks, facing the Chetniks between Travnik and Novi Travnik. True, the HVO was better armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. Djidic, were most of the Territorial Defence fighters at the line, up on the line in either Visoko or Mont Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in late October, these events you testified to occurred in and around the 20th October, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In late October the Bosnian Serbs took over Jajce; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did that change the relationship between the Territorial Defence and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did, and significantly so. After the fall of Jajce, that means when the Chetniks occupied Jajce, there began even more intense negotiations, discussed with the HVO wherein they no longer require disarmament. The meetings are more moderate in tone, and we reach an agreement only 10 days after the conflict, to organise a joint defence against the Chetniks. We made good moves forward. In that period, October, November, December, more precisely November and December, the agreement I mentioned yesterday was reached, between Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Merdan, announcing movements of the army, to announce, more precisely, the movements of the army, to not have the army remain for longer periods of time in one place, and to know the exact time and the number of people moving towards a certain location. All in all, the situation improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me direct your -- you are talking at this point about improvement between October and November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, let me direct your attention to approximately 20th November, 1992. On that date, did you have any telephone conversations with the accused Tihomir Blaskic or with another individual by the name of Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, around 10 pm, I received information that two members of the Territorial Defence were killed and one was injured. That happened in the settlement named Krusica. They were killed by members of the HVO. Some time around 11 pm, or maybe midnight, Pasko Ljubicic called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Who is Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pasko Ljubicic was commander of the regional police of the HVO. The regional military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue with what you were saying, Mr. Djidic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pasko asked me about members of the military police, whether they had been captured and where they were at the time. I did not know their whereabouts, so I consulted some people in Krusica who told me that they had captured, I think it was six members of the HVO, in retaliation for the killing of two members of the Territorial Defence. As I had been asked to have them released, I ordered the HVO fighters to be released. However, it was very difficult to achieve this. People in Krusica demanded an investigation into the killing of the TO members so that they would find out who it was who had killed them, and if they were given promises that such an investigation would be carried out, then they would release the HVO fighters. I spoke with Mr. Ljubicic again and told him that the fighters had still not been released, but that they would be released. In response Ljubicic said that he would, together with members of the regional police and with the military, begin to arrest Muslims, one by one, to arrest and detain them; and about 3 am I spoke to Mr. Blaskic, who gave me an ultimatum, and said unless the HVO fighters are released by 8 o'clock in the morning he would surround Krusica and attack it. After that, I managed to obtain assurances and promises from Mr. Merdan that an investigation would be initiated, but that the fighters had to be released. I guaranteed, with my life, to the soldiers in Krusica that an investigation would be undertaken to find out -- to identify the killers the very next morning, and that they must release the HVO members immediately. That is what they, in fact, did, about 5.30 am. At 6 am I called up Mr. Blaskic to tell him that the fighters had been released; and his reply was: "Yes, they have been released, but they were beaten up." And then he said if by 9 o'clock we do not tell him who had done that that both my headquarters and Vitez would be set on fire. But it was not, then, on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, carrying on with the story, Mr. Djidic, were soldiers of the TO arrested for beating up these HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The very next day Mr. Merdan came to my headquarters. We went to Krusica together. We found the people who had beaten the HVO fighters. We found the things that had been seized from them, and they were returned to their owners; and two TO members were taken into custody in the prison at Zenica. Mr. Dzemal Merdan took them there himself together with the Zenica police. They were tried and they served a prison sentence. From the HVO we never received any feedback regarding what had happened to the killers of the TO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At any point did Pasko Ljubicic or Blaskic tell you there would be some investigation into the murder of these TO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall them saying that to me, but I assume that Mr. Merdan must have talked to one of them, since he did give me assurances that an investigation would start in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, after this particular incident, Mr. Djidic, were you personally upset about this series of events? And if so did you attempt to do anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was extremely upset, so were all the people in Vitez; and at the time of intensified negotiations with the HVO we tried to set up a joint unit, that is to line up Croats and Muslims together and send them to the front against the Chetniks. And I proposed something to that effect to Mr. Cerkez, but it was not accepted. We went to the front against the Chetniks separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Djidic, the name of the unit that these HVO members who had been captured by the TO and Krusica were a member of? Do you recall which part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were members of the Regional Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Under the command of Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Mr. Djidic, was an investigation of the murder of the two Territorial Defence soldiers ever conducted, and was anybody ever arrested and prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I know of. I never received any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, carrying on from there, into December of 1992, what is the state of the relationship between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats in the Vitez area coming into the new year, the new year being 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, that was a period of quite successful negotiation. There were even proposals for all the people of Vitez to be mobilised from one spot, that is by the Defence office, so that the call up calls for TO members should bear the stamp of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and for Croats the calls -- the papers calling up Croats to carry the stamp of Herceg-Bosnia. That new location would have to be found for the TO headquarters, as my accommodation was most unsatisfactory. Meetings were held with the highest ranking officers of the army and the HVO, so that together we could march against the Chetniks. I already noted that in those days we no longer had problems regarding collection of weapons, nor in connection with demands that we had to place ourselves under the HVO command; but each side went to the front independently, without there being any problems between us. Notice was regularly given of people being deployed on the front, and, at the time, a ban was in force on wearing long -- carrying long rifles in town. This applied both to HVO members and TO members, because the HVO and TO members would frequently, returning from the front, shoot, and disturb the population, the inhabitants. So, there was a definite improvement of relations between the HVO and the TO, or rather between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, Mr. Djidic, and if we can move up a little bit until January of 1993 and the events that took place in Busovaca. Did the fighting in Busovaca have some impact on the relations between the Muslims and the Croats in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. When, after the fighting in Busovaca, the people were very seriously disturbed, and apparent peace still prevailed in Vitez, but in Busovaca a conflict was going on. Certain problems occurred when the HVO set fire to a village, which is on the border between Vitez and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What village was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the village of Kovacevac and Pezic. In the immediate vicinity of Gornja Rovna and Vranicka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were the HVO soldiers in Vitez involved in the fighting in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally saw HVO soldiers passing along the road to Busovaca. I even saw a 20 millimetre anti-aircraft gun, which was on a truck, being driven in the direction of Busovaca. And whether they participated in the fighting, I do not know, because I did not eyewitness that. I did observe, however, on several occasions, passenger vehicles, private cars, and vans, and trucks of the HVO transporting fighters in the direction of Busovaca. I also saw some soldiers driving in certain things from Busovaca. These were mostly household appliances and TV sets. I do not know where they got them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when you saw these HVO soldiers carrying in household appliances and TV sets, what did you think -- where did you think they had gotten these items, and how did you think they had gotten them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first I did not know, but I learnt later that they were things that had been stolen from the Muslims in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, where were you when you observed these HVO soldiers bringing back looted property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in Vitez, on the road leading to my house, because I went to and from work daily; and one could notice this in the day time, and particularly so during the night, these movements became more frequent, because my house is on the main road leading to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, while this was going on in Busovaca, was there relative peace in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. The HVO was extremely polite. We had friendly conversations. The idea was that we should not interfere in the problems in Busovaca, that this would -- settlement would be found locally, and we, from Vitez, did not indeed interfere in the problems of Busovaca, as far as the TO is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you detect a certain philosophy or approach by the HVO to try to have peace in one area where the -- while the HVO was moving into another area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. That appeared to have been the policy of the HVO, to maintain the peace in one town or in several towns while capturing another region or another town. This was a well known tactic from the previous conflicts that had occurred in Vitez and Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During these events in Busovaca, was there any request on the part of anybody from the HVO concerning coffins for the people in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, at a meeting, we had at the mayor's, the mayor, Ivica Santic said that he had received requests from Busovaca for a large number of coffins. What he meant was that we, in Vitez, needed to co-operate, so that we would not go through what the people of Busovaca were going through. I do not know what his purpose was in saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it clear to you, Mr. Djidic, that the coffins he was asking for were coffins for Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After January of 1993, and the situation in Busovaca, did the situation in Busovaca calm down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell the court what exactly happened after the situation in Busovaca calmed down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the conflict in Busovaca came to an end, there were very many Muslims who had been evicted from their homes; but an attempt was made, by political means, again, to come to some kind of an agreement and to stop the conflict. And that time, I think, an agreement was actually signed between President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic on peace and co-operation, and in central Bosnia joint teams were working, joint teams of the HVO and the army, whose task it was defence against the Chetniks. This situation continued until the month of April when, at several meetings, it was noted that we needed to wait for decisions to be taken at the political level concerning central Bosnia, or Bosnia-Herzegovina as such, and that we should concentrate all our effort on the struggle against the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did things change in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, things changed, and dramatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you tell the court what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of April, the old problems re-emerged regarding disarming army members, houses were broken into, cars were confiscated, some kind of wild checkpoints, irregular checkpoints were set up by the HVO, and at these checkpoints most Muslims were looted. And the situation became worse by the day. At the same time, negotiations continued, and somewhere around April the 13th we reached a stage when we were talking about a joint police force, joint patrols, that would cover the whole territory of the municipality of Vitez. We were given assurances, by both the political and military leaders of the HVO, that a war would never break out in Vitez between the Muslims and the Croats. That we need to live together, to work together and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What members of the HVO military and the HVO political sides gave you these assurances? Do you have any names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specifically Mario Cerkez, who was invited to come as a guest -- I beg your pardon -- to attend Army Day celebrations which were held on April 14th. He would say such things on April 15th, similar statements were made by Mr. Samija, who was, at the time, head of the civilian police in Vitez, to Mr. Saban Mahmutovic, who was chief of police in Stari Vitez. Those statements were that all problems have been resolved, that there would be no war, and that we have a happier future to look forward to; and many Muslims believed this. However, that was not how things turned out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did any Muslims change their behaviour or change their homes as a result of these promises by the HVO that there would be no fighting between the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One of them was Saban Mahmutovic, whom Samija convinced that there would be no war, that everything was fine, he went to the country, to the village of Sadovaca, his native village, and brought his family to Vitez, and he spent the night in Vitez. And the attack started the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit 45, where in Vitez did he bring his family back to, if you could point to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This here (Indicates) is Saban Mahmutovic's house. It is about 200 metres from the hotel, and 150 metres from the cinema.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Hotel Vitez being the headquarters of the accused, Blaskic, and the cinema being the headquarters of Mario Cerkez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: While you are standing there, Mr. Djidic, could you point out on the Prosecutor's Exhibit 45 the area of Vitez known as Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The colony or Kolonija is this part (Indicates), these apartment buildings here (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And on that map again the area of Stari Vitez is below Kolonija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. This is Stari Vitez (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, if you could be seated again, please. Now, you said, Mr. Djidic, that you received these assurances from Mario Cerkez on the day that you celebrated Army Day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who was Mario Cerkez's commanding officer when he was making those assurances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His commanding officer was Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall what date it was that the TO or the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina celebrated Army Day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the 14th April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After the celebration of Army Day, were there any other meetings concerning co-operation between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims prior to the morning of 16th April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a meeting of a commission, a commission for the preservation of peace, for dealing with incidents in Vitez, of which both Mr. Samija and Mr. Saban were members, as well as some other people. And they agreed, on that day, that they would, again, the next day, on April 16th, have a meeting to agree on certain concrete issues, such as joined police patrols. Of course, that meeting never took place, because of the attack in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take us to the morning of 16th April, 1993. What happened, Mr. Djidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This might be the best time to take a break. We will resume at 11.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, and Mr. Kehoe, before we continue with the examination of the witness, there is an organisational point for our hearings, which means for rules which are related to other cases in this Tribunal, and only one Trial Chamber, there is a new change for tomorrow which I will tell you now. Tomorrow morning we will be able to meet for the Blaskic case from 10.30 until 1 o'clock. Then from 2.30 until 4 o'clock. And after that there will be another hearing. But -- no, I did say 10.30. It is 10.30. Again I repeat, the Blaskic case 10.30 until 1 and then 2.30 until 4. Let us hope there is no other change. I will be sure there is no other change. Pardon me for this. Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, your Honours. Mr. Djidic, my last question was turning to the events of 16th April 1993. Can you tell the court what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 16th April 1993, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean the day before, or exactly the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about the day before, and then going into the 16th. Where were you, what were you doing? What was happening? Then begin to explain the events of the 16th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 15th April, 1993, there were many detentions and arrests of members of the army, as well as Muslim civilians. One of my officers was arrested at the HVO checkpoint, at the turning point on the road towards Novi Travnik. His vehicle was seized and he was detained, imprisoned. In that prison he saw many other civilians and members of the army. Those civilians and members of the army were also -- had also been arrested in Vitez and were detained in the school building in Dubravica. In the course of that day I managed to come to an agreement with someone from the HVO to have my officer released, and indeed he was released, some time in the afternoon, but he did not get his vehicle back. The people who were imprisoned in the school building were not released that day. We had extensive discussions, trying to obtain the release of the people from the school building and the station, but we did not manage to get that. The night passed rather peacefully, without any incidents; and then the next morning, at 5.40 am I received a message saying that the village of Ahmici was attacked. When I left my headquarters and went outside, I could distinctly hear the shooting, and I saw smoke rising. Houses were burning. Around 6 am the attack on Stari Vitez began. The entire territory of Stari Vitez was under shellfire, and was attacked from all types of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Using the map that is, or the photograph that is on the easel, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 56, can you point to the various locations from which Stari Vitez was shelled on the morning of 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Indicates) this area, the area of Stari Vitez, was shelled from the direction of Krusica (Indicates) from the direction of Mlakici (Indicates) from the direction of Gradina (Indicates) and from other positions, from heavy guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What type of heavy weaponry are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am talking about cannons of a higher calibre, 105 millimetre cannons, multiple rocket throwers -- launchers, 128 millimetres, and mortar shells of all calibres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, could you, when you were in -- let me withdraw that question. Could you point on the map where your headquarters was in Stari Vitez on the morning of the 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My headquarters (Indicates) was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, on the morning of the 16th, could you hear where this shellfire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From where the shellfire was, again, where is the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most frequently the shelling came from Grbavica, from Ahmici, from Gradina and smaller cannons, 20 and 40 millimetres in calibre, shelled from the direction of Kolonija and from the direction of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, if you could when you point to something on the map could you just hold it there for a minute while the cameraman just adjusts the camera. Now, when Stari Vitez was shelled at 6 o'clock in the morning, were any other areas in and around Vitez being attacked at the same time, and if so could you point those areas out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time we could hear shellfire, and we also received messages about shelling against Krusica, against Ahmici against Busovaca, a part of Donja Veceriska, then Dubravica, the Subrino Selo village, Porcurica and Preocica. All those are villages around Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were areas within the Vitez town itself also being attacked, in addition to Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some time around 9 o'clock I talked on the phone with an officer from the headquarters who is sleeping in his own apartment in Kolonija, not far from the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where is Kolonija on Exhibit 56?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates) This area here, near the hotel, and this is his apartment building (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to the middle of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is approximately where the apartment of the officer I was talking to was situated. He wanted an ambulance vehicle and he said he and his wife were injured. During that conversation we were disconnected, and about an hour later I was informed that this man had been killed, and so was his wife. The killings took place in his apartment before their children -- before their three children. I also received messages to the effect that Muslims were being killed in their apartments in Vitez and that arrests were being made of Muslims in the location of Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before you continue Rijeka is the area just up to the left from Kolonija on the road going out, going out of town. What did you learn about what was going on in Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received information that Muslims were being arrested, and taken to prison, located at the veterinary station. I had no further contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, before we move on, if we could just clarify the typed record and the photograph that you are reviewing, which I believe is Prosecutor's Exhibit 56. The area of Krusica that was being attacked is on the upper right-hand side of this photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is Krusica (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the area of Donja Veceriska is down in the lower right-hand corner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is it (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the area of the factory, where the shelling was coming from, is the lower right-hand corner as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you said that shelling was coming from Crkva, and that is on the left-hand side of the photograph; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so, it is here (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Djidic, you may have a seat, sir. So in the morning of the 16th shelling is coming from Crkva, the factory, Donja Veceriska and Mlakici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mlakici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the same time Muslims have being arrested and killed in Kolonija, Rijeka and Ahmici is on fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on this information, did you, as a military officer, reach any conclusions as to whether or not this was a co-ordinated attack by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was obvious. The entire territory of the municipality of Vitez was under attack, and the attack had all the features of infantry attacks, shelling, arrests of Muslims, in the most part of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At what time of day, sir, did you get the telephone call from Ahmici that it was under attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was exactly at 5.40 -- 5.45, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what time of the day was Stari Vitez shelled or when did the shelling begin of Stari Vitez on the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 6 o'clock, 15 minutes after Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it clear, sir, those artillery pieces were in position prior to the attack of Ahmici at 5.30 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This attack was taking place, the shelling of Stari Vitez was taking place from various locations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it clear to you at the time that the shelling of Stari Vitez was a co-ordinated attack that was planned prior to the attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could notice that the area under shellfire, after the first wave of shelling was subject to infantry attacks. That means that almost simultaneously in the greatest part of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning our attention back to Prosecutor's Exhibit 56, the overhead photograph. From what directions did the infantry attack come from after the artillery attack subsided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stari Vitez was attacked from three directions, from the direction of Crkva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to the bottom of the half of the photograph, moving up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the direction of Mlakici (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are moving from Mlakici from right to left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Mlakici towards Stari Vitez, and from the direction of Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is moving from the centre of the town down the photograph into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You can have a seat, sir. Now, Mr. Djidic, how many soldiers did you have in Stari Vitez at the time of this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of the attack there were approximately 50 to 100 soldiers in Vitez. They were deployed. They were accommodated in one room, in one building called the fire fighting house. And some soldiers and officers were in the headquarters, in the building which I pointed out. A certain number of soldiers were in their own houses, resting; and another set of soldiers was on the front line in Visoko and in Vlasic, since at that time, during the winter a brigade was formed. There was also a number of soldiers from that brigade who were residents of Stari Vitez, resting after their time at the front. And on that day they were in their own houses in Stari Vitez. Those were the only two military buildings in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many civilians were in Stari Vitez at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 1,600 residents of Stari Vitez then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that morning of the 16th April, did you expect to be attacked, Mr. Djidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not expecting that attack. I did not anticipate it; and I was taken very much by surprise. And so were all the residents of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why did you not expect the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not expect it because intense negotiations and discussions were underway, agreements had been reached and assurances given, that there would be no war in Vitez. Not a single member of the HVO had been arrested in Vitez; and there was no reason for that attack, although the situation was tense because of the arrests on the eve of the 16th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Speaking of arrests, there had been an arrest in Crkva, was there not, of an HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt that -- I learnt about that on the first day of the attack, when a meeting was set up with the HVO, with the participation of members of the UNPROFOR. I heard that an officer of the HVO was arrested, Zivko Totic, and that the army had arrested three HVO soldiers, in the -- in Opara, near Novi Travnik. All these locations are outside Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, going back to the attack on Vitez, on the morning of the 16th. You said it was after the artillery fire that an infantry attack started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know what units in the HVO participated in these infantry attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about that. At that time I did not know what units were involved. The soldiers who were seen by my own soldiers and the locals were dressed in different uniforms, in camouflage uniforms, black uniforms. Quite a few of these people were wearing headgear covering their faces, and painted with black paint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take us through, Mr. Djidic, the rest of the morning of the 16th. The artillery fire started at approximately 6 o'clock in the morning. Just take us through, time wise, what happened the rest of that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 7 o'clock I received a message but I could also see it for myself that from the direction of Kolonija five or six houses were set on fire. Those were Muslim houses, and they were burning. Ten or so Muslim houses were set on fire, from the direction of Veceriska and from the opposite direction. A man from Stari Vitez came to my headquarters and told me that the HVO broke into his house, that they wanted to kill him and they set his house on fire. That house was in the immediate vicinity of the barricade held by the civilian police in Stari Vitez. That is where the HVO soldiers were stopped. Panic reigned in Stari Vitez. First there was shellfire, houses were burning, then came the infantry attack. It was a madness. People did not know where to hide. On that day members of the army did not have a single trench in Stari Vitez. They hid behind houses and local buildings, and from those positions resisted the attack. No one, including myself, could possibly anticipate such an attack. Then the wounded started coming in. They were admitted into the local infirmary; and around 10 o'clock the first victims, the first casualties were recorded. Infantry attacks and occasional artillery attacks continued throughout the day with brief remissions in moments when Stari Vitez, when members of the UNPROFOR reached Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were civilian houses being burnt during these infantry attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the houses that were set on fire on that occasion were civilian houses, without any significance, nor could there be any doubt that they might be military facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you said that these homes were of no significance, they are of no military significance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on with the day. You said that the infantry and artillery attacks continued throughout the day. Was there some intercession made by the UNPROFOR during the course of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the course of the morning my headquarters was hit. So we had to change location. And when UNPROFOR members came there would be a slight lull in the firing, though fire could still be heard in the distance, on many sides. Particularly, at that time while UNPROFOR forces were in Stari Vitez, HVO snipers continued operating continuously. Life in Stari Vitez was brought to a total standstill. People were terrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there a cease-fire agreement organised or an attempt for a cease-fire agreement organised by the British battalion during the course of 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The officers of the British battalion managed to organise a meeting which was attended on the part of the HVO by an officer called Zoran Pilicic. He was a staff officer in the operative zone. I think he stood in for Mr. Blaskic. And another officer, called Marko Prskalo. The wish of the British battalion was to achieve an immediate cease-fire. And the HVO officers said that Zivko Totic had been captured in Crkva and some other HVO fighters in Novi Travnik, and if they were not released the attack would not cease. Vitez had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on with this meeting. What was the end result of the meeting at BritBat on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The final outcome was that we agreed on a cease-fire, and that we should meet again the next day at the UNPROFOR base to see what had been accomplished regarding the cease-fire, and the cessation of hostilities. In the course of the night UNPROFOR set up several checkpoints, and said it would patrol Stari Vitez and Vitez, in the desire to stop the hostilities, even though fire was opened against them. Major Brian Walters said that they had not returned fire because they had come to achieve peace. And he asked us that each one of us should issue orders to our respective armies not to fire at UNPROFOR vehicles. It was stated on that day that HVO fighters had fired at warriors in Ahmici when members of the British battalion went to see what was happening there. This was confirmed by the commander of the British battalion at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the course of these meetings -- the meeting on the 16th, did Marko Perskalo make any statements as to why the HVO was using artillery against Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I said that artillery shells were falling on Stari Vitez and the surrounding localities, Marko Perskalo said that the HVO was using its artillery because allegedly members of the army had shelled HVO positions. And it was clear that that was not true, though later on there was an exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why initially was it clear that that was not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was visible as most of the shells were falling on Muslim villages, or rather the villages where the majority of residents were Muslims, and also on the area of Stari Vitez, which it was not difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on. What happened after this meeting in BritBat ended on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the day the infantry attacks ceased. A shell or two would fall on Stari Vitez. From time to time a sniper was fired, but mostly the damage that had been done was repaired, and we tried to find accommodation for the people whose houses had been burnt down with owners whose houses were still standing, though on that first day many houses had been visibly damaged from the shelling of Stari Vitez. In fact, the whole area of Stari Vitez. The night was more or less peaceful, with some isolated shots. And then the infantry attacks on Stari Vitez resumed on the 17th. Usually those attacks were accompanied by heavy artillery fire. It was obvious that the HVO wanted to capture Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Djidic, after this cease-fire agreement on the 16th the artillery fire began again on the 17th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the soldiers and the other citizens of Stari Vitez attempt to defend themselves at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the second day defence lines were formed. People stood behind their houses and various other buildings on their farms, without any real shelter or any trenches. At the same time, as the attack on Stari Vitez on the 17th, the village of Novaci came under repeated attack, and it is in the immediate vicinity of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If Mr. Djidic, could you go back to what has been introduced into evidence as Prosecutor's Exhibit 56 and point to the area of Novaci and hold the point there for a moment so the camera can pick it up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This here is the village of Novaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is the area, the village that is to the left of Vitez or Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see that village being attacked on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it. The attack continued and one could clearly hear the shooting. It is about 500 metres from Stari Vitez, a part of the village is on a slope, on a hill, and one can clearly see from Stari Vitez when someone is moving in that part of the village. There again houses were burning both on the first and the second day. During the night, and the second day some 40 men fled to Stari Vitez who did not want to surrender; and their families stayed behind in their homes, which will -- they were later captured, and they were put up in the cellars of -- cellars of houses and in the prison at the school building in Dubravica, those people who entered Stari Vitez stayed there throughout the war, and they never saw their families until the truce was signed, and they helped me a great deal in the Defence of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After those men fled, what happened to -- and their families were taken prisoner, what happened to the Muslim homes in Novaci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of the Muslim homes were set on fire, not all the houses, however, they are still standing. Not a single house owned by a Croat was burnt down. They are still standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you see those Muslim homes on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is on the 17th. Are there any other meetings on the 17th at BritBat that you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about those, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A meeting held on the second day, I do not exactly know where, it was also attended by HVO members. The subject discussed was more or less the same, how hostilities could be stopped. I had received a report that many Muslims had been captured. I demanded their release, and if possible that they be allowed to go to safety, so that they should no longer be captured. Already on the second day I knew what had happened in Ahmici. I heard the news from local people who had fled, and also from members of the British battalion. And the second day came to an end without any success being achieved in halting the fighting. And on the third day we went to a scheduled meeting at the UNPROFOR base in Bila. Present at that meeting, in addition to myself, was the deputy commander of the 325th brigade, and Mario Cerkez, on behalf of the HVO. As a second HVO member was not there, I did not attend the meeting, but waited in the hallway. The meeting lasted roughly two hours. And roughly about 4.30 pm I heard a strong powerful explosion. As I was in the UNPROFOR base at the time, I could see clearly from that position a large cloud of smoke and I could conclude from that that the explosion had occurred in Stari Vitez; and this was confirmed later. This big explosion was from automobile bomb, a car bomb, which contained between 4 and 5000 kilograms of explosives. When it went off the entire area of Donja Mahala was destroyed, Donja Mahala in Stari Vitez. On that occasion, five civilians were killed, one member of the army, and more than 50 civilians were wounded. And with the assistance of the UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross they were evacuated to the UNPROFOR base in Bila. After that explosion, it was a day of great sorrow in Vitez, a day of extreme panic, with the hosts of wounded people, killed and very many houses destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Djidic -- Mr. President with the court's permission, if I can move into the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 81, with the assistance of the usher. Again, Mr. President, with the court's permission if we could again have the usher assist the witness with the ELMO and the photographs it would be helpful to move through these photographs expeditiously. (Handed). Mr. President, with the court's permission again if I could ask the usher to stand by Mr. Djidic and possibly assist with the ELMO it would be very helpful. Before we move to these photographs, Mr. Djidic, after the explosion in Stari Vitez -- after the explosion in Stari Vitez on the 18th April, 1993, did you ride back in the same warrior with Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was his reaction to knowing that there had been an explosion in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the participants in the meeting came out, they were dumb, silent, nobody said a word. We climbed into the same warrior, Mario, his escort, myself and Sivro Sifet. He was the deputy commander of the 235th Mountain Brigade. We all went to Stari Vitez. I got out of the warrior. The warrior went on in the direction of the colony. That is where Mario and his escort probably got off. And Sivro Sifet was driven to Krusica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So Mario Cerkez never made any comment at all about the explosion in Stari Vitez during your entire trip back to Stari Vitez, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a word. Nobody said a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to Exhibit 81. And the photograph that is on the ELMO for the record is PH238. This one on the ELMO. What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This picture shows a Muslim house which is closest to the church in Stari Vitez. The shot was probably taken on the first day of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning our attention, Mr. Djidic, back to the photograph, could you orient the court where on the photograph this picture is taken, if you could step up to Exhibit 56, which is the overhead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is this house, here (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you are pointing to a little more than half way down the photograph, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The church is here, and this house is here (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, is this a Muslim house or a Croat house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a Muslim house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You be seated, sir. Let us turn our attention to the next photograph, PH257, if we may. Do you recognise that area, Mr. Djidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Stari Vitez, Donja Mahala, the spot where the same vehicle exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next photograph, PH258. If we could take that out of the sleeve and put that on the ELMO. Do you recognise that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same spot where the car bomb went off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, are these houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Kehoe, since it is almost 1 o'clock and we have not finished with this photograph album, if you do not mind we could resume at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The court is adjourned until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume our hearing. Please have the accused brought in

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes your Honour, Mr. President your Honours, good afternoon. I believe we were talking about PH257. Is that the photograph that is on the ELMO at this point? Is that the one that is on? 258 we are on the next one, okay. Talking about PH258 again, what is that Mr. Djidic? What area does that depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the areas of Stari Vitez, the place where the car bomb exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Djidic, you did not take these photographs and you were not present when they were taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, and I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next photograph, PH259.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph also depicts the place of the explosion and the houses surrounding it, inside Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, were these civilian houses or were they military installations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of these are civilian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the next photograph, which is PH237.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you see here are the remnants of the truck, the cistern which exploded in Stari Vitez, only a small part of it remained. The rest was blown up in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, is this photograph taken from the direction of the Hotel Vitez down towards the church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the other photographs that we were looking at were taken from the direction of the church towards the Hotel Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, are these civilian houses in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of these houses are civilian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next photograph, PH243.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a civilian house in whose immediate facility the cistern exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was anybody killed in this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A civilian male was killed here, and a young girl.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, how many people were killed and how many people were wounded as a result of this truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think six people died as a result of the explosion, five of them civilians and one serviceman. More than 50 others were injured, 50 civilians, most of them were evacuated with the help of the UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross, immediately after the explosion, and they were moved to the British battalion's base in Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us start with the next photograph, 260.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is one of the demolished houses in whose vicinity the car bomb exploded, that is in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next photograph, PH263.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you can see several houses which were destroyed by the car bomb explosion, that is in Stari Vitez, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djidic, was the mosque in Stari Vitez destroyed or harmed or damaged in any way by the truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mosque was damaged. To be more precise, the explosion damaged its roof, and the window panes were destroyed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you turn to the next photograph, PH263? The next photograph, if you could put that on the ELMO. PH262. They are not necessarily in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the mosque at Vitez. This part here, the roof, had not been damaged before. Part of the roof in this photograph has already been repaired, and new window panes were put in. But you see here (Indicates) is the minaret which had been hit. It had been hit by some sort of a cannon from the direction of the column or Kolonija, and that happened either in October or perhaps November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in 1992, in the course of the first, very first conflicts which were short lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the roof itself is damaged with the truck bomb on 18th April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now all of these photographs, sir, do they -- while you were not present when they were taken -- do they accurately reflect the damage to Stari Vitez as a result of this truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the pictures do. This particular one, the picture of the mosque, was made some time after, not on the day following the explosion, and you can see that the tile has been changed. This entire side (Indicates) had the tiles damaged. This photograph was taken after some repairs had already been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay sir. Now, in your prior statement you said that there were snipers shooting into Stari Vitez on 16th April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the sniper attacks continue through the entire time of the siege until the cease-fire in February of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The snipers were shooting all the time, with the exception of very few days during the truces, when exchanges of prisoners or cease-fires had been scheduled. But even the cease-fires were often broken, so that always, at all times, one could be hit by a sniper, and people could not move round freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you hear, if you were in the Vitez area, could you hear sniper fire? Was there a unique sound to sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could, and I did hear it, and I was not the only one. Everybody heard that. A sniper fire has a characteristic sound. Those are individual shots directed at targets in Stari Vitez. Such a shot was usually slightly louder than a normal bullet. They were most usually -- they were most often two shots together, and especially characteristic, especially typical of sniper fire when they used a higher calibre sniper the shot was even louder than that of a normal sniper. What was used in Stari Vitez was snipers of 9 millimetres, 10.5 millimetres and 12.7 millimetres. That is anti-aircraft machine gun. Of all these snipers we had casualties from all of these snipers. Most of the casualties were not only soldiers but civilians, regrettably the civilians were usually old people, and even children. The youngest child to be killed by sniper fire was only two and a half years old. And all the old people that -- who fell victim to sniper fire were over 60. Another child hit by a sniper of a higher calibre was 8 years old. I still remember these images. They are fresh in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the next two photographs, Mr. Djidic, starting with PH337, if we may. What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first building outside Stari Vitez. We used to call it the yellow building. It is from this building that the snipers shot from the direction of Kolonija, and the same is true of the building next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the final picture in that exhibit, which is PH340.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the yellow building I described, photographed from a greater distance, from Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is taken from Stari Vitez looking towards Kolonija and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher could we flip down the first photograph, then, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 45? If we could clip that down. Mr. Djidic, using Prosecutor's Exhibit 45, could you point on that photograph where these photographs of the yellow building are, the buildings where the sniper fire came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the yellow building (Indicates), and this is the building next door (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that would be just up to the left of the football field; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. How far is that location away from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 50 metres away, sorry 50 to 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you were in the Hotel Vitez or around the Hotel Vitez through the entire time of the siege, would you hear this sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Have a seat, sir. Your Honour, at this time the Prosecutor would offer into evidence Prosecutor's 81 and with the assistance of the usher we can put that exhibit back together again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are there any comments? Perhaps I was not paying attention, but I do not think that you identified the person who took these photographs, Mr. Kehoe. There are some with inscriptions on them which seem to say they are official photographs. Perhaps I was not paying close enough attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These photographs, your Honour, were taken by British soldiers, from the Cheshire Regiment and also from the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire. Many of those individuals will be testifying in this regard, and certainly this exhibit is available for additional examination by the court of those officers. I raise it in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is fine. Thank you very much. This is 81, then, is that not right? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, is it not Mr. Dubuisson? Mr. Djidic, after the truck bomb went off on 18th April, 1993, what happened? What happened with regard to the conflict with the HVO? Were other areas attacked, that you saw? Tell the court what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the truck bomb explosion, which occurred on the 18th April, the village of Gacice was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can stop you with the assistance of the usher if we could again move back to Exhibit 56 and allow Mr. Djidic to stand up and identify Gacice. Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This area here (Indicates) is the village of Gacice, which is only 400 to 500 metres away from Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir, you can have a seat, please. Did you see this attack of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I observed that attack. I saw soldiers moving from the direction of Mlakici and surrounding the village of Gacice. After some time, there was shooting, fierce infantry shooting. One could occasionally hear a bomb or a grenade. I cannot -- I could not say exactly. And then, houses were set on fire, one after the other. In approximately an hour's time about 20 houses were burning in the village of Gacice. The people who were with me confirmed that the burning houses belonged to Muslims, and that turned out to be true later. The following day I learnt that the HVO occupied the village of Gacice, that civilians were detained and imprisoned and a number of men managed to flea to the nearby woods. From the woods they later moved to the village of Krusica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on all of the attacks in Vitez and the attack on Kruscica and Gacice what did you think that the HVO was trying to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO's objective, their purpose, was to kill and destroy the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Bosnian army's servicemen, to kill and destroy civilians, and civilian targets, civilian property, and to ethnically cleanse the City of Vitez, and they achieved that objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ethnically cleanse Vitez of what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You saw the attack of soldiers running down the road going to Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you recognise these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not recognise them. Those were mainly soldiers dressed in camouflage or black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now were there various units in the Lasva Valley that were part of the HVO that were dressed in black uniforms and in camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one unit wearing black uniforms, and that was special unit of commanders called Knights, or Vitozovi in Serbian, but there were members of the HVO other units wearing black uniforms, not as many as among the Knights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about the Vitozovi, what was the Vitozovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitozovi are a unit of commanders, otherwise it was an unit of the HOS, Croatian Armed Forces, on the territory of Bosnia. That unit later changed its name from HOS to Vitozovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When they changed their from HOS to Vitozovi did they begin to work with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitozovi, or the Knights, had special premises in the school building in Dubravica. A part of them were accommodated in the school building in Travnik, but they always worked together with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was the leader of the Vitozovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was headed by their then commander Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to the conflict, on 16th April 1997, had you seen Darko Kordic with any of the HVO military leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would see him, frequently, in the company of Mario Cerkez. They were friends and -- anyway. I would also see Darko Kordic, actually I saw him on October 20th, when my logistics base was attacked in the hotel, in the HVO command building; and I learnt later that he personally had participated in the attack on the logistics centre and the TO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are referring to the hotel, you are referring to the Hotel Vitez, Blaskic's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Also in the valley was there a unit called the Jokeri?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. It was also a special unit, special task force, like some kind of military police, with a special purpose. They were housed in the hunting lodge opposite Stari Vitez, and a part of that unit was housed in the motel known as bungalow in Nadioci in the immediate vicinity of the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After the attack on Gacice what happened with regard to the continuing conflict between the HVO and the BIH, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several days later the situation seemed to have calmed down. A number of meetings were held between members of the army and the HVO. A joint group was set up, headed by Mr. Sefer Halilovic who was, at the time, chief of staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Mr. Petkovic, as the highest ranking officer in the HVO. There were several other officers from the army and from the HVO. The task of this group was, through the mediation of UNPROFOR, to put an end to all armed hostilities and to try to restore peace. They also had, as one of its goals, the release of all prisoners, and bringing relief to all victims. That group came to Stari Vitez perhaps 10 days after the conflict first broke out. The documents from that meeting I have handed to the Tribunal, or rather a video cassette on that meeting. It was requested at that meeting that hostilities cease and that all civilians be released. I did not have any captured civilians in Stari Vitez. All the Croats who had lived in Stari Vitez were in the cellars, together with the Muslims. And this could be seen on the spot as this joint team, when it toured Stari Vitez, was able to see. At the time, there were about 80 Croats in Stari Vitez. They were offered the possibility of crossing over to the new part of Vitez, to the Kolonija. Some of them agreed, but most of them remained in Stari Vitez, to live there with the Muslims, as before.
