There was a total of 45 Croats, and 3 Serbs who stayed in Stari Vitez throughout the war; and most of them are still living in Stari Vitez. This commission went from Stari Vitez to the hotel. I did not go to the hotel. And I do not know what they discussed there. After the hotel they visited the cinema, and I had been informed that a large number of Muslim civilians had been imprisoned in the cinema. I do not know the exact figure, but not only in the cinema, but there were captured Muslims in other places, as well. And they were told that they would be released; that each one of them should state where they wanted to go, and this exchange actually occurred. I think it was the next day. I requested guarantees from this joint group for the people who were staying on in Vitez, guarantees that they would be safe, because there were no members of the army in Vitez. We were given these assurances, guarantees, but the people who were released then were expelled from Vitez during the next three or four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After this exchange did you see any individuals coming back into Stari Vitez, as part of this exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw about a dozen males who came to Stari Vitez. Some of them had houses in Stari Vitez. Some of them had apartments in Vitez; but they came to Stari Vitez to stay with their parents. There were some who brought along their wives and children. I knew them all. I spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you look at their hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And it was interesting because one of the men complained to me that the HVO had forced him to dig trenches. His hands were full of blisters, and they were bloody. This was a man who was a guard in the factory when I was in charge there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see anybody digging trenches while you were in Stari Vitez? Could you look in the outlying area and see anyone digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see the digging of trenches in the area around Krcevine and I saw that it was a civilian digging a trench. There were soldiers there, too, but I cannot claim what ethnic group that civilian belonged to because I could not see his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you say that the trench digging was taking place around Krcevine, can you use Exhibit 56 and point once again to Krcevine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This part here (Indicates). All this is known as Krcevine. I saw the digging of trenches somewhere here (Indicates). It is about 800 to 900 metres from Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. After this visit from General Halilovic and Petkovic did there come a time when the citizens of Stari Vitez buried their dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you tell the court about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The corpses were collected. The volumes of civilians who had been killed in Ahmici, in the Kolonija and in Donja Veceriska. The HVO wanted to bury them at the City Cemetery in Vitez, but the people from Stari Vitez insisted, and I supported them. It was agreed that these people be buried in Stari Vitez. I think this was 12 days after the beginning of the conflict, through the mediation of UNPROFOR the HVO permitted us to bury those people. The people who were members of the Civil Defence in Stari Vitez went to Vitez to the school where the dead were placed in one of the rooms, tied, tied up into long bags. The transportation -- transportation began and all the dead were transferred to Stari Vitez. I think that 105 corpses were buried on that day in Stari Vitez. More than half of those corpses could not be identified, although the HVO carried out the identification. I was personally present when the identification process began. I saw three corpses, and I could not look any more. The corpses were mostly massacred. They were burnt up, and there were bodies of babies to old men. There was only one or two of those corpses that was in uniform. The rest were all civilians. It was a day of the greatest mourning in Vitez. Everybody was crying, everybody, even UNPROFOR. Those strong men, it was really very hard. After that, and after the funeral there was no peace, even that first night. The HVO snipers continued their actions. The war continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After the bodies were buried in Stari Vitez, did the siege of Stari Vitez that continued until February of 1994 begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. People were hoping that this would come to an end soon, but having learnt from the experiences of the previous conflict, no one believed that a neighbour could do something like that to another neighbour. Up to that point in time, up to that funeral of those people, I had considerable problems, for people to dig in. They did not want to, because they thought it would be over soon. But when they saw the funeral of these people, women and children, then they hurried themselves to dig holes as deep as possible where they would be able to hide during offensives, which occurred almost daily against Stari Vitez. One day after another I managed to reinforce the line of defence, to set up a system of circular defence, and it was with those lines that I saw the war come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that from late April of 1993 until February of 1994 Vitez, Stari Vitez was surrounded and under siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Stari Vitez was totally surrounded, and there was absolutely no way out of Stari Vitez, nor could anyone come in, nor could anyone go out, could leave Stari Vitez. The moment we had buried the civilians the army swore not to leave the people and to defend them to the last man, though I could have made a break through from Stari Vitez, and could have pulled out, together with the members of the army. And the civilians appreciated this decision of mine, and the decision of their closest family and friends, because members of the army were their husbands and fathers and sons who were protecting their homes and their families. There were only a few refugees from Jajce there. The rest were all residents of Vitez, and we knew what our task and our aim was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, tell the court what life was like in Stari Vitez during the period of the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Life in Stari Vitez during the period of the siege was very difficult. We had many problems. We had wounded civilians, destroyed homes. Every day several buildings would go down. There was a problem to find accommodation for these people, so that in a single small cellar there would be up to 100 civilians, people lacked clothing. Many houses had been burnt down, or ruined by explosives which were used in Stari Vitez during the siege. We had very little food and it was all of the same kind, no vitamins or any spices or fat. A large number of people aged rapidly under those conditions. We all lost weight. People were losing their teeth. People suffered from stress. And we had a 5 year old child whose hair turned grey. That photograph has toured the world. Simply, life was intolerable, and I ask myself how we managed to survive, despite so many difficulties, which the whole world was familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, were civilians killed during the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell the court how civilians died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the civilians were killed at the beginning of the war, five of them, when the car bomb went off. Most of the other civilian casualties died from HVO snipers. I already said that among them were children, women and old people. Some of them survived and if they had been evacuated and taken to a hospital, but because no adequate medical attention was available maybe in some cases a glass of blood would have been sufficient to save somebody's life. However, being in Vitez they were condemned to die.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why were they condemned to die? Why were they not permitted to be taken out to get adequate medical care?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know why they were not given adequate care. A number of people were evacuated, and they survived, though there were others who died. But in most cases, when I asked for evacuation I had to indicate the name of the injured person, and one could clearly see if it was a child or a woman or an old man. When the International Red Cross did not appear, then they would say, in a couple of days, that they were sorry that they could not come, but they would also add that the HVO did not allow them to enter Stari Vitez. In the meantime, the people for whom we had asked assistance had already died, so it was too late for them anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was the HVO commander when you received the information that the HVO would not allow you to evacuate wounded? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time the commander for central Bosnia was Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about the siege. Did the artillery attacks stop after April of 1993, or did they continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the artillery attacks stopped, probably because the HVO ran short of shells. But they resorted to something else. Towards the end of May they started to use explosive devices which were very destructive, with a lot of explosives and their aim was the destruction of personnel and buildings in Vitez. Those devices were made from fire fighting equipment; and between 6 and 10 kilograms of explosives could be put inside. And these were fired by the HVO, with a handmade catapult. And the whole territory of Stari Vitez was targeted. Those devices were also made to be incendiary and later on, during the war, we noticed that this device was being fitted with pieces of steel, or nails, screws, various other iron objects, so that there would be more pieces to make them more lethal. And this, of course, was a source of great concern, a large number of buildings were destroyed. And they caused great fear among the civilian population. As a result of these devices, houses were destroyed, everything was killed in the immediate vicinity where this device fell, and people suffered from very serious stress syndrome, because when 10 kilograms of explosives went off the noise was terrible, and it was a horror. Those devices were fired at us from May till February, at any time of the day or night. And I can say that more than a thousand of these devices fell on Stari Vitez. It is not hard to calculate how much explosives that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These particular explosive devices were in fire extinguishers, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I believe the word you used to describe them were "babies"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what we used to call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall an attack using these babies on the 18th July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall it very vividly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Talk about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 18th July, 1993, there was a general -- an all out attack of the HVO against Stari Vitez. We were attacked in the small hours, and the fighting lasted all day, almost 12 hours. The HVO's purpose was to penetrate Stari Vitez before the infantry attack. There was shelling from various artillery weapons, and about 200 devices which we called babies were fired, covering -- and the shellfire covered more than a half of the entire territory of Stari Vitez. In the course of the day, when infantry attacks came one after the other, another hundred of these devices were fired, all falling on the territory of Stari Vitez and causing great damage, injuries to a great number of civilians. There were also injured soldiers in my units; and when the attack was over, somewhere by the end of the day, only then could I appreciate the extent of the damage. I could hardly believe it. After that battle, after that attack, there was not a single building left undamaged in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Civilian buildings, civilian homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, civilian homes, but also my line of defence. The device we called baby was very difficult to handle, to control. You never knew where it would fall, because this launcher does not have a name. It should approximately, in the general direction of the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So would it be accurate to say, Mr. Djidic, that the HVO fired approximately 300 of these explosive devices, having no knowledge where they were going to land, because you could not aim them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where were they fired from, on 18th July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From various sides. Most of them came from the direction of Sirka, or the church, from the direction of the factory from Ahmici, from the kindergarten, from opposite the hotel where there is a platform in front of the school building, and from the woods on one side of Stari Vitez. You can say they came from all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, when these babies were being fired at Stari Vitez, Blaskic was the commander of the central Bosnia operative zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, if I could turn to what is marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 82, I believe Mr. Dubuisson, is that correct, 82? And with the assistance of the usher I would like to review with you, Mr. Djidic, some of the weaponry that was used against Stari Vitez during the time of the initial battle, and also the siege, including the sniper attacks, and the babies. Just by point of clarification when you mentioned that they were being fired from the direction of the hotel, you were referring to the Hotel Vitez, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, with your Honours' permissions, if I could ask the usher to stand with Mr. Djidic and place these individual photographs on the ELMO so that he could explain them. The first photograph is part of Prosecutor's Exhibit 82 is Z2-461. Mr. Djidic, do you recognise that? Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this. This is an anti-aircraft gun of 40 millimetres calibre. You see it placed on a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see a weapon such as this in and around the Stari Vitez area during the time of the HVO attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw it around Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think somewhere in Krcevine. And this vehicle was moving and carrying this gun. It means that the HVO often changed the position of this gun. The soldiers understand very well why position is frequently changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon such as this in Stari Vitez during the siege, at any time during the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never had such a gun in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have ammunition in Stari Vitez during the entire siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the siege we had ammunition for the weapons that we had at our disposal, mainly infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, what calibre is this weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 40 millimetres, an anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the next photograph, Z2-462.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the same gun, photographed from a different angle, placed on a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is a placed on a truck to remain mobile, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the next photograph, Z2-463. What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is an anti-aircraft gun of 20 millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Have you seen any of these in and around the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw something similar to this. That is an anti-aircraft gun, a triple anti-aircraft gun, which the HVO had even before the war. It was also placed in a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to Z2-467, which is the next photograph. What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a house (Indicates) and this here I think is the launcher of devices we call babies. This is the cat from which these -- catapult from which these devices were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can move up three photographs. If we could move three photographs up, it is a little out of sequence, if we move up three photographs I believe those photographs follow. 467 should be followed by 466. Do you recognise that, Mr. Djidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This used to be a fire extinguisher, and -- but now it is an unexploded baby, a device which did not detonate and it was sent to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct me if I am wrong, this particular fire extinguisher would be placed in that launcher we just saw and then fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How would it fly through the air? Would it fly through the air like a missile or would it tumble?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Its line of flight was irregular. It was very noisy and it tumbled, and that is what usually saved us, because you could very clearly hear when it was fired. Then it went up into the air, tumbling, and made a characteristic noise (Demonstrates), that you could not mistake for anything else. So people knew exactly where it was heading, and they hid, if it was in the day time. Those who are inside houses could not know where it would fall; and in every house hit by this device everybody was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you tell the court about any instances, and examples of when these babies hit houses and killed all the civilians in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you of two typical cases. In one house, near the stadium, a baby hit an old house where eight civilians were injured. Of those eight two women over 65. They were sisters, and they were killed. On another occasion, a baby hit a house inside which four women were killed at the same time; but by a twist of fate two small children survived. Unfortunately they were mentally disturbed for life. One of the four women killed could not be found by us. We only found shreds of her clothes. In a corner we found her foot; and that is all that we managed to find. That was really a horror.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, let us turn to the next photograph, which is Z2-464. What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a mortar, 120 millimetres in calibre, or perhaps 82 millimetres. But I would say rather 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were mortars of this calibre or approximate calibre used against Stari Vitez during the attack or the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were, especially in the first days, in the early days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the next photograph, Z2-465. What is that, Mr. Djidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a multiple rocket launcher, 128 millimetres in calibre; and we were shelled from this gun too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When were you shelled from this gun, this type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mainly in the early days of the conflict that we were shelled, during the siege, and also in February, towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn to the next photograph which is Z2-468.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you see here is a glycerine gun, and it is called a glycerine gun because it fires small grenades, small shells filled with nitro-glycerine and it is mainly used in battles in settlements, inside settlements. Its effect is rather psychological than military, rather psychological than destructive. In a closed space its power of destruction is great.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was this glycerine gun used during the battle in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the weapons used, but I would say -- I would call it ridiculous after the big guns, after the heavy guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. Let us turn our attention to the next photograph, Z2-469. If you can look at the two photographs, Z2-469 and Z2-470 one after another where you have the same weapon in the individual's left hand, that large weapon in that individual's left hand, what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you see here is a sniper, 12.7 millimetres in calibre. It is a high calibre sniper, and it was used against Stari Vitez, and I can claim, with a great degree of certainty, that at least three civilians were killed from this weapon, and several were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you give the court an example of some of the three civilians that were killed with this weapon or this type of weapon, a 12.7 millimetre calibre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. One of the civilians killed was a young man named Boris. He was a driver for the UNHCR. He was hit by this bullet. The bullet penetrated his chest and went out, hit the hinge of the door of, of the car door, and stopped there. After the ballistics’ analysis conducted by the UNPROFOR it was established that the shot was fired from HVO positions from a 12.7 millimetre calibre sniper. I saw that bullet, from the same side from which the said Boris was killed, a woman was -- a woman over 65 years old was killed in her own garden in front of her house, while she was pumping water. She was shot in the heart. It was later established that the bullet was of the same calibre. An 8 year old child was hit from the same weapon right in the heart, but the bullet came from the opposite side. A number of other civilians, women, were hit from this weapon, but luckily they stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next photograph Z2-1470. That is the same weapon that we were discussing before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same. Yes, it is the same weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That has got a scope on it, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what is the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To destroy human beings. Snipers of this kind were frequently used for elephant and bear hunting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is the accurate range of this weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what its range is, but with this sniper it is possible to hit any target with great accuracy at a distance of 1000 metres and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn over to the last photograph, Z2-471. What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also an anti-aircraft machine gun, without a sniper. I think it is also 12.7 millimetre in calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was this the same type of weapon that you were describing earlier as being used against Stari Vitez as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a similar weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecutor will offer into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 82. These photographs have been taken by various members of the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, would you please allow Mr. Kehoe to finish, then I will give the floor to you. You wanted to finish with the identification of the photos before we give the floor to the Defence to hear his objection. Is that all you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I wanted to complete the identification for the court's purposes these were taken by the members of the Cheshire Regiment, as I stated previously members of the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire. That is who provided these photographs to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then they should be put under 82. Mr. Hayman, do you want to express an objection? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Only as to Z2-463, your Honour. The witness was not able to identify that as a weapon he was familiar with concerning the battle, if you will, the siege of Stari Vitez and the fighting in that area. So it may well be a witness later on can authenticate it, but I think that one photo has not yet been connected to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I do not really see any objection to having it be part of the exhibit. We have taken into account your objection. You can raise this again during the cross-examination, but I do not see any problem having all these documents be put into the case under number 82. It is now 5 minutes after 4. We will break until 25 minutes after 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Please be seated, have the accused brought in (the accused was brought in).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President? A point of clarification Mr. Djidic. You stated that the truck bomb attack took place on 18th April. When approximately did the attack on Gacice take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A day, or maybe two after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the sniper attacks, can you give the court an idea of how many civilians were actually killed from sniper attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the effects of sniper attacks, in Stari Vitez, at least 10 civilians died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about from the attacks of artillery or babies, how many civilians died in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least 15 civilians, at least -- that is the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many civilians were injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez more than 200 civilians were injured. Some people were wounded several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the siege, between late April and 1994, were you and the individuals in Stari Vitez supplied by the Bosnian government or by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as the Bosnian government is concerned, and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we did not receive absolutely anything. All that we received was food, through the mediation of the UNHCR; and this was mostly limited to flour, lentils and rice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the same period of time were the HVO being supplied? And do you know how?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frequently we could see convoys of trucks with food, and when these convoys arrived in Stari Vitez the HVO would prevent them from entering Stari Vitez, and then the UNHCR suspended deliveries of food to the HVO as well. However, Stari Vitez was totally under siege for about 100 days, when we did not have a single visit by anyone, nobody could come in or go out from Stari Vitez. We were simply being -- we had simply been abandoned, probably to see how long we could survive without food; and at the same time the HVO was supplied from the air. Helicopters would bring ammunition, weapons, food and probably troops, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see these helicopter flights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every time the helicopters flew into Vitez we could all see them, or hear them. If it was foggy, so they could not be seen, we recorded more than 100 flights coming in and out by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During this period of time when no one could come in or out of Stari Vitez, were the sniper attacks continuing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the sniper attacks -- were the sniper attacks directed towards livestock as well as humans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The sniper attacks were directed against everything that moved in Stari Vitez, anything that lived, both human beings and animals, so that several cows were killed, several sheep, which provided milk for small children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going back again, you mentioned the fog. Did the fog have any effect on Stari Vitez and how you tried to work around the sniper attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Vitez is well known for its fog. Even in the summer we may have a day of fog, because it is situated in the valley of the Lasva River. In order to survive, the local people of Stari Vitez worked in their gardens at night and early in the morning. And sometimes they would not notice that the mist had lifted and they would be hit by HVO snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The husband and wife that were close to 70 years of age that you have mentioned before, were they in their garden when they were hit by snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, both of them were in the garden. They were digging the garden for potatoes. They were killed within a period of 1 hour, one from the other, in the same garden.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can turn my attention to what has been marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 83. With the assistance of the usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, do you think that you will be finished by 6 o'clock today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I do. (Handed). Moving through these photographs, Mr. Djidic, as part of a Prosecutor's Exhibit 83, I believe that is correct, is it not, Mr. Dubuisson? 83. The first photograph is PH236. Before we go to that you said in the latter part of April 1993 the bodies from Kolonija, Ahmici and other areas around the Vitez area were buried in the graveyard of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning your attention to the first photograph, what are we looking at here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph shows the burial of the people who had been killed in Ahmici, Vitez and Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where are they buried in this photograph, can you point to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is in the immediate vicinity of the mosque in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These wooden markers coming out of the ground, what are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each of these wooden planks is placed above the head of the dead man. It has a number on it, and then you know who was buried where, at least as far as those who were identified are concerned. Then there was a separate slab in the corner of the cemetery, indicating names of those that we knew, and the number from this wooden piece of wood, or plank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn to the next photograph, PH242.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are also part of the digging during the funeral of the mentioned people. A bulldozer of the UNPROFOR helped us to prepare the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn to the next photograph, PH261.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you can see the laying of the bodies of the killed in the ground, in the tomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next photograph, PH241.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the same cemetery that I was talking about, after the funeral was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those photographs were from the funeral in April of 1993. I would like to turn your attention to PH319, the next photograph. Is that a photograph as to how the graveyard looks today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is the outside -- sir, can you describe the set up of this graveyard, with the gravestones on the outside and the gravestones in the middle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This line that you see (Indicates) in the back is where the people from Ahmici were buried. There is another row of those markers that cannot be seen. In the middle here were people who were killed during the siege, during the 11 months of siege. Most here (Indicates) you see members of the army were buried, and the people killed by explosive devices and snipers. The civilians who died of natural causes were buried in the cemetery next to the mosque, within the courtyard of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us take the next two photographs, PH267 and PH266. You were talking before about a chart with names and identification of those individuals. Is this what you were talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the slab I had referred to. Here we see the numbers, indicated on the markers, then, if we know the names, they are written there, and those that were not identified it just says MN, it may be a man or a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Put the PH266 on the ELMO, if you could. There are several unidentified bodies enumerated on that page, are there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are quite a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move on to the next one, PH268. You can look at that, all three together, PH268, 269 and 270 and 271 and 280. If we could just move through those in sequence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the numbers (Indicates), indicated on the chart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same. The photograph also shows the markers with the numbers (Indicates). Photograph 271 more markers with numbers. This photograph also has markers with numbers on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving to photograph PH272, could you put that on the ELMO, sir? Some of these individuals have names on theirs such as 48 Japcic Salem. Do you recognise that man, that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is a man killed in Vitez in the Kolonija, and he was a member of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was killed in front of his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about 49 and 50, the ones right next to them, the two gravestones next to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 50 is the tomb of Sali Sadbasic. He was an elderly man. He was killed on the first day of the attack, near the church, during the identification it was established that his throat was cut, probably with a knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know how old he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was over 70, maybe even 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about the number 49?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could also be a man killed near the church. I think he was a younger man, and there is another spot, another Sadbasic, an elder man his father, this one's father. They were killed together on the first day of the attack, near the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you turn to the next photograph, PH274? You mentioned an individual who moved back to Vitez after the meetings on the 14th and 15th April, because he was comfortable with how things were going between the HVO and the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is so. Yes. Here you see the tombstone number 66, where Saban Mahmutopic lies buried. He was chief of police who trusted the stories told him by his colleague Samija. He went to the Kolonija with his family, and in the next day or two he was killed. He was killed in the street, like a dog.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next page, PH275. Here the individual -- do you know the individuals in gravestone 71 and 72?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Salja Omerdic is number 71. I knew the man. He was a civilian killed in the Kolonija. Next to him this white tombstone is a tombstone to Mira Zlotic. She was a Serb married to a Muslim. She worked as the treasurer in my staff. It is the woman, if you remember when I was testifying about the killing of her and her husband in the apartment, in the presence of their three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to PH276, the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This white tombstone, it is not really a tombstone, just a marker, is the place where Nedem Zlotrg was buried, the husband of Mira Zlotrg I was just speaking about. And I spoke to him on the phone, when he asked for an ambulance the first day of the attack. This marker here (Indicates) is a tombstone of a lawyer, Mirhet Varupa. He was 44 years old. He also was killed in his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: A civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to PH277.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see here the tomb of an old man who was killed in Donja Veceriska. I think he was over 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: A civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next page, 279.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name you see here, under number 88 is Jrafeta Haskic the wife of the man I just mentioned. She was also over 70. She was killed in Donja Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next page. Next photograph, PH293. The gravestone on the right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This gravestone is the grave of a civilian killed in his house when the truck bomb exploded. His house was the closest to the spot where the truck bomb went off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next photograph, PH315.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This gravestone -- the tomb contains parts of the body of the man who drove the truck bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Had you concluded, based on talking to people in the area, that the person who drove that truck bomb was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We learnt that later, from people who were exchanged. He was a refugee from Hrkonjic Grad who was captured and held in the prison at the school near the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who had him drive this truck into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was forced by HVO soldiers. That was the report I received. Apparently the soldiers asked: "Are there any volunteers who know how to drive a cistern truck?" If he manages to pass with the truck through Stari Vitez he would be released. And this man volunteered, and ended up in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next photograph, PH314.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you see here is the grave of a boy who was killed by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about the one next to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the grave of a woman who was killed by an explosion, I think she was over 70, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was she likewise a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to PH300, and the gravestone on the left side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an inscription of the name of the civilian who was killed together with this boy, by an explosion and the grenade fell from the direction of Krcevine on to a house with civilians in it. They had just come out of the house from the cellar to breathe some air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next photograph, PH291. The gravestone on the right side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the grave of the third man killed by the same grenade. He was a serviceman. His house was right next to this one (Indicates). When he was killed he was not in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many civilians were killed in that explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three civilians were killed by the same explosion, and six were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us get down to the next photograph, PH289.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we see a grave of a civilian, an engineer. We called him "Dedo" as an endearment. He was hit by a sniper because -- and he could not be evacuated after he was wounded, by the morning he was dead from his injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That paragraph is PH309. Why could he not be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO would not allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the photograph PH289 Abdic Mursad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a member of the army hit by a sniper. Again, in this case, the HVO would not allow evacuation. He died two days after he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next one, PH299.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where an 8 year old boy is buried. He was hit by a sniper in the street. The sniper was of a higher calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is this the young boy that you mentioned previously that was hit with the 12.7 millimetre round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the boy. I am not sure if it is a 12.7 or a smaller calibre, but he had both a penetration and the exit wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What were the size of those penetration, or more importantly what was the size of that exit wound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The size of the penetration wound was about 1 centimetre in diameter and the exit wound was about 10 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you draw any conclusions based on the calibre, or attempt to draw any conclusions based on the calibre, based on the size of that exit wound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. One could conclude that it was higher calibre weapon or a dispersion bullet, which is also banned by the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn to the next photograph, PH283.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you see here are two graves of a mother and daughter who were killed in their house by an explosive device. Another two women were killed on the same occasion, if you remember when I spoke of four women killed inside a house. This is the mother, and this is the daughter. The only body part we found left of this woman was a foot, and small pieces of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn to the next photograph, PH302.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the third woman killed in that house, her name was Patkovic Katica. She was a Croat, married to a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the last photograph, PH288.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the grave of the fourth woman killed in the same explosion, also civilian. All of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: All four were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Killed in the same explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were killed by the same explosive device which exploded in the room, and it fell inside the room through the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the room of the house, that is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When did this take place, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that happened in December, perhaps January 1994. I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be approximately January of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I will offer into evidence what has been exhibit, the exhibit we have just been discussing, Prosecutor's Exhibit 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, this is Exhibit 83. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the entire siege you stated during your examination that Stari Vitez continued to be attacked with these babies and occasionally with sniper fire and with infantry fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take you to early September of 1993. Were you in a position to see the attack by the HVO on the village of a Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where is Grbavica, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is north of Stari Vitez, a kilometre, a kilometre and a half distance. It is very clearly seen from Stari Vitez, and I observed the attack on Grbavica. I could see clearly what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Looking at the Prosecutor's Exhibit 56 would it be fair to say Grbavica is just off the bottom of that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this photograph you cannot see Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am saying would it be just outside the bottom part of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere here (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you observed the attack on Grbavica in September 1993 what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attack went on for two days. On the first day there were artillery attacks using explosive devices, so-called babies. We saw them flying through the air. And on the second day I saw houses burning. At first I thought there were set on fire by ammunition, flammable ammunition, but it was a mistake. I looked more closely and saw soldiers, and not only soldiers but also civilians who were looting houses in Grbavica, probably even then, as early as then the army had retreated from Grbavica. When they took whatever they wanted to take from the houses they set them on fire. At one point, one could see over 100 houses on fire. All of the houses belonged to Muslims. Only a few houses belonging to Muslims escaped this fate in a village which had over 200 houses. I think that on that day the mosque also burnt in Grbavica, but the minaret survived until the end of the war. It was not demolished, but it was eventually demolished and destroyed in 1994, when the truce had already been signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was the burning of the houses in Grbavica consistent with the pattern of burning Muslim houses throughout the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seemed so. Houses would first be looted and then set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continuing on, sir, after September of 1993, up until the end of the siege in 1994, did the siege stop? Were Muslims free to travel in and out of Stari Vitez throughout the winter of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The Muslims from Vitez were allowed to come out freely until June, all those who were refugees in Stari Vitez, and the HVO made no trouble for them then. But evacuation of the wounded was a problem with them. The International Red Cross gave guarantees as was their duty, that after first aid and treatment of the evacuated persons families would be reunited in Stari Vitez. Again, those people were not allowed, on most occasions, by the HVO, to return to Stari Vitez. Only very few people were reunited with their families in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How did the siege end, Mr. Djidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The siege ended on 25th February 1994, by virtue of the signing of the Dayton Accord. However, 10 days earlier fierce attacks were made against Stari Vitez. Those were combined attacks, artillery and infantry attacks, using huge sound effects and using the broadcasting of specific songs, shouts, appeals for surrender to the members of the Bosnian army. Two or three sentences would be read over the public address system, and then the artillery attack would follow. And that went on for several days. The time from 21st February to 25th February, in that period we saw the fiercest attacks on Stari Vitez which continued in waves, and they used the entire range of artillery weapons they had at their disposal -- I mean the HVO -- in order to capture Stari Vitez. The fighting went on for three days. The last attack took place on the 25th, at 4.15 am. Around 8 o'clock infantry attacks ceased. At noon the truce came into force. No more attacks against Stari Vitez followed after that. It is noteworthy that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the course of those two or three days of attacks against Stari Vitez were issued orders that there would be no offensives launched, and there were none indeed. Nobody even helped us, apart from the artillery support that we had. It seems to me that we were left to our own devices in those three days. We were left in the lurch, and to be captured by the HVO. Thank God and thank people who defended Stari Vitez, the HVO did not enter Stari Vitez. After that there came the signing of the Accord and the end of the war. Thank God, since then there has been no more shooting in Vitez. A meeting was held at the UNPROFOR base, where we signed the maps, demarcation maps, indicating lines of the demarcation between the HVO and the Bosnian army. That meeting was attended by high ranking officers, including Mr. Blaskic. That was when I saw him after a long time, and to be truthful, I must say, at that meeting when the signing took place we shook hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, this is the end of hostilities. Have the Muslims moved back to their homes throughout the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. No, your Honours. To this day not a single Muslim has returned to Vitez. The Dayton Accord, especially Annex 7, is not observed in Vitez at all. Certain efforts are being made to achieve something, but there are still people obstructing the implementation of the Dayton Accord; and although this Accord proclaimed a federation in which Muslims and Croats live together and form the majority, but also the Serbs, in Vitez and especially in Vitez nobody has returned to their home yet. In other places there are certain improvements, a great number of Croats returned to Zenica, to Travnik, to Gugojno. A number of Muslims returned to Jajce, to Zepce, to Srolac and to Busovaca, but none to Vitez. And in conclusion of my statement, I kindly ask you to do your utmost to prevent this crime from ever happening again and to help as much as you can, if that is at all possible, to help me live in Vitez again, together with my neighbours, Croats and Serbs, who are alive. I would like us to live in one state again, because we have no other state but Bosnia. Please do not allow, if you have such a mandate, do not allow such crimes to be repeated anywhere on this earth again. Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, just going back again, you are familiar with this area, and you are familiar with the Hotel Vitez and the entire Vitez area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the morning of 16th April 1993, from the Hotel Vitez, could you see Ahmici, a smoke from Ahmici, and could you hear the gunfire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I had been in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would have seen that. That could be seen from Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you were in the Hotel Vitez would you see the attack taking place on Kolonija, and hear that attack taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Pucarevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Donja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that could be heard and seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Several days later Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if you were in the Hotel Vitez you could see virtually all of the activity taking place on the attacks of these villages, and hear the gunfire and the shelling of those villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shooting would be heard from hotel room, it could be seen. But it could neither be heard nor seen if a person would -- if a person had been in the cellar, but only in that case could they fail to see and hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Throughout this entire time of the siege of Vitez and all these attacks, including the attacks on Stari Vitez from April of 1993, through February of 1994, who was the commander of the HVO for that area, for the central Bosnia operative zone?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Asked and answered, your Honour. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained. You have asked that question -- you have asked the question several times and it has already been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment, Mr. President. (Pause). Mr. President, I have no further questions of Mr. Djidic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djidic, the examination has now been concluded. It is 5.30. We will resume tomorrow morning at 10.30. Let me remind you about the morning's hours that is 10.30 to 1 then 2.30 until 4 o'clock for the cross-examination. Do you expect to finish tomorrow, Mr. Hayman? You think that you will finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, your Honours, we will do our best to complete the cross-examination tomorrow, but, as you know, we are not allowed to cross-examine, both of us, so that we will need some time for consultations amongst us, and especially if we do not know in advance the witness that is taking the stand, it complicates matters. But we will do our best to complete the cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that, Mr. Nobilo. The court stands adjourned until tomorrow at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: on Wednesday 30th July 1997)
